children: By Ron Bousso
Record-high US diesel prices were in President Donald Trump's crosshairs this week amid his campaign to ease the cost-of-living squeeze ahead of November's midterm elections.

Facing pressure from Republican lawmakers demanding action to curb the soaring costs of the critical fuel, Trump on Tuesday threw his support behind the idea of restricting diesel exports. Just a few words from the president were enough to send global oil and diesel markets into turmoil. The strong reaction reflected the critical role the US plays in the diesel market, particularly since the start of the Iran war, which has taken a huge share of global refining capacity off the market.

By Wednesday afternoon, the White House was partly rowing the president’s statements back. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration was not pursuing an outright export ban and was instead working with refiners to boost domestic supplies in a "simpler, voluntary, cooperative fashion." He offered no specifics and stressed that no decisions had been made.

Global markets were unconvinced. While a diesel export ban might deliver a short-lived drop in US prices, it would almost certainly create bigger problems elsewhere and ultimately lead to even higher prices in the United States. Find out more in my latest column.
THE DIESEL DILEMMA

Diesel rarely grabs headlines like crude oil or gasoline, but it remains one of the world's most important fuels. It moves goods from factories and farms to stores and construction sites, making it a crucial ingredient of modern economic activity.
That helps explain why markets are so nervous.

Global diesel supplies were severely disrupted as the Middle East conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war have knocked out refining capacity around the world. Diesel prices around the world surged in recent months to record highs, while retail US diesel prices soared to a record $6.50 a gallon.

The US oil industry has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of those two conflicts. As supplies from Russia and the Middle East became more constrained, US producers stepped in, sharply increasing exports of crude oil, refined fuels and LNG while capturing hefty profits in the process.

Before the conflicts, Russia and the Middle East together supplied roughly one-fifth of global seaborne diesel exports. Today, the United States alone accounts for about the same share after lifting diesel exports by more than 20% this year from 2025 levels to around 1.3 million barrels per day, according to Kpler.
But success abroad has come with a catch.

US diesel inventories have fallen to their lowest level for this time of year in more than four decades and are about 13% below year-ago levels. The decline is especially worrying because stockpiles would normally be building ahead of autumn refinery maintenance and the winter heating season.

An export ban would pile pressure on import-dependent economies. Mexico, Chile and Brazil are the biggest buyers of US diesel and together take more than a quarter of exports. Europe accounts for roughly another quarter.
Those customers were quick to grasp what was at stake.

Benchmark European diesel prices jumped more than 5% on Wednesday, while refining profits climbed towards recent record highs near $90 a barrel. In the United States, prices and refining margins moved sharply lower as traders began pricing in the possibility of export restrictions.
The problem is that the world does not have much spare diesel to fall back on. Global refineries are already running flat out, leaving few alternatives if US supplies suddenly dry up.
